newsitem.title: MAURITIUS: Growing world sugar refining capacity worries EU.
newsitem.headline: Growing world sugar refining capacity worries EU.

text.p: The European Union (EU), one of the world's biggest white sugar exporters, is concerned about some countries' potential to increase refining and production, an EU official said on Tuesday.

The official, who is attending an International Sugar Organisation (ISO) meeting in Mauritius, said the recent building of a sugar refinery in Saudi Arabia, a major market for EU products, was a worrying development.
"If this is going to be symptomatic of a more substantial move in the world...then clearly that is going to have implications for world trade," said the official, who asked not to be identified.

"There is going to be less demand for exports in refined sugar and more pressure on people to send raw sugar into refineries in countries like Saudi Arabia instead of into refineries in places like Europe," he said.
He was, however, uncertain whether more mills, which require a hefty capital outlay, would be built in the Middle East region in the near future.

Sugar traders in London last month said that EU sugar was facing tough competition from new and planned refineries in the Middle East, especially Dubai's Al Khaleej plant at Jebel Ali which has an annual capacity of 720,000 tonnes.

The EU official also pointed to a substantial hike in sugar output in Thailand which in the 1995/96 year produced 6.38 million tonnes of raw sugar. The ISO has predicted the Asian country will lift output to 6.50 million tonnes in 1996/97.
Brazil also has the potential to upset global sugar trade, the EU official said.

"They have massive sugar production and a large amount goes into ethanol, so they really only need to reduce quite a small percentage of their ethanol production and that liberates substantial quantities of sugar onto the world market," he said.

Earlier this month the Austrailian Sugar Convention heard that Brazil had the potential to become the world's most powerful player over the next two decades if it stopped pumping nearly 60 percent of its sugar cane into the expensive production of ethanol for motor vehicles.
Czarnikow's latest sugar estimate puts Brazil's 1996/97 production at 14.775 million tonnes, up from 13.594 million a year ago.
